Home
hom
n. and adv. (one's own dwelling; the place of belonging; rendering Hebrew bayith, Greek oikos and idios)
From the Saxon ham, a dwelling, village, or estate — surviving in English place-names ending in -ham. Unlike house, which names the structure, home has always named the belonging: the house one returns to.

Biblical Definition

Home in the Authorized Version is where a man belongs and returns, and Scripture gives it three uses worth distinguishing. First, it is a place of witness. The delivered Gadarene begged to follow Christ, and was refused with an errand instead: “Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee” (Mark 5:19). The first mission field is the house one came from, and the first congregation is the people who knew the man before. Second, it is a place of duty, and the Lord himself provides one from the cross: “And from that hour that disciple took her unto his own home” (John 19:27). Dying for the sins of the world, he does not overlook the housing of his mother. Paul reasons the same way when he charges widows' children to shew piety at home before anywhere else (1 Timothy 5:4); religion that has not yet reached the household is not ready to be exported. Third, and most soberly, home is used of the grave and of heaven. Ecclesiastes says of the aged that “man goeth to his long home” (Ecclesiastes 12:5), and Paul balances the two dwellings: “whilst we are at home in the body, we are absent from the Lord” (2 Corinthians 5:6). That verse quietly unsettles every earthly hearth. The believer's present address is a temporary one, and the homesickness he cannot explain is accurate.

Webster 1828 Definition

One's own dwelling and place of belonging. Scripture makes it the first mission field, the first field of duty, and — against every earthly hearth — the place the believer is not yet at.

expand to see more

HOME, n. [Sax. ham, a house, a village.] A dwelling house; the house or place in which one resides.

2. One's own country; as, to return home from a foreign land.

3. The place of constant residence; the seat of family or of domestic life.

4. HOME, adv. To one's habitation or country; as, go home; return home.

5. Closely; to the point; as, to press an argument home; the reproof came home to him.

Key Scripture

Mark 5:19 — "Howbeit Jesus suffered him not, but saith unto him, Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had compassion on thee."

John 19:27 — "Then saith he to the disciple, Behold thy mother! And from that hour that disciple took her unto his own home."

Ecclesiastes 12:5 — "Also when they shall be afraid of that which is high, and fears shall be in the way, and the almond tree shall flourish, and the grasshopper shall be a burden, and desire shall fail: because man goeth to his long home, and the mourners go about the streets:"

2 Corinthians 5:6 — "Therefore we are always confident, knowing that, whilst we are at home in the body, we are absent from the Lord:"

Modern Corruption

Home is reduced to a private refuge from the world — a place to be comfortable rather than a place to be faithful — while the believer's real homelessness in this world is quietly forgotten.

expand to see more

The modern house is sold as a sanctuary from obligation: a place where a man is finally off duty. Scripture reverses this. Home is where duty is densest, because it is where the people are whom God has actually given us to serve. Timothy is told that piety is proved at home before it is displayed anywhere else (1 Timothy 5:4); the Lord in his dying hour secures a roof for his mother (John 19:27); and the healed man of Gadara is sent home precisely because the hardest audience for a testimony is the household that remembers the man in his chains. A Christianity that is impressive in public and slack at its own table has failed the first examination.

The principle to recover is Paul's uncomfortable arithmetic: whilst we are at home in the body, we are absent from the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:6). Both halves are true at once. The Christian is genuinely at home here — God gave him this body, this house, these people, and gratitude is the right response — and he is genuinely away from home, because the Lord he loves is elsewhere. Ecclesiastes calls the grave a man's long home to make the same point from the other side. Comfort here is real; permanence here is not.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew bayith serves for both house and household, structure and family together. Greek oikos is the house and those in it; idios, one's own, gives the sense of home in several passages.

expand to see more

Hebrew bayith (H1004) — house, household, family; the structure and the people are one word.

Hebrew ohel (H168) — tent, dwelling; the patriarchs' home, portable by design.

Greek oikos (G3624) — house, household; the root of oikonomia, stewardship of a house.

Greek idios (G2398) — one's own; rendered home where the sense is one's own place.

Greek endemeo (G1736) — to be at home, to be among one's own people; the verb of 2 Corinthians 5:6.

Usage

"Of the first mission field: go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee (Mark 5:19)."

"Of duty provided from the cross: that disciple took her unto his own home (John 19:27)."
